statement: How a death enters a count of drug deaths depends on the country, the register and the period, so figures from different sources do not count the same thing, and studies that matched the same deaths across two sources found that they overlapped only partly. In US national statistics for residents who died in the US, a drug overdose death is one whose underlying cause on the death certificate is coded to ICD-10 X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent); deaths from long-term drug effects and from side effects of medicines taken as prescribed are left out. A drug counts as involved when the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner, wrote it in Part I, Part II or the injury description, unless the words around it say otherwise, and a death with several drugs is counted under each of them, so the 15 drug-specific counts for 2023 added up to 179,965 against 106,352 deaths (editors' arithmetic); the National Center for Health Statistics calls its drug counts minimums and says that the certificate cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026). ICD-10 codes put different drugs together (fentanyl and tramadol share one code; oxycodone, morphine and codeine share another): in Washington State in 2003–2010 one code covered 2,725 poisoning deaths; its most often named drugs or terms were oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine and opiate. These names overlapped within deaths and were not an exhaustive list; the certificate's words could separate names that the code grouped together (Ossiander, 2014). The certifier's words also decide whether and how a death is coded: a US consensus panel convened by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration notes that 'acute cocaine intoxication' is coded as a poisoning while 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded as a mental and behavioural disorder (Goldberger et al., 2013), and 'drug overdose' with no drug named is coded as unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). The same panel separated deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which a drug was only detected (Goldberger et al., 2013). European registers differ again. Norway's Cause of Death Registry, under the European (EMCDDA, now EUDA) definition, counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden, a national selection counted a listed drug code anywhere on the certificate, the European selection only the underlying cause from a shorter list, and a forensic register any death in which an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause, at ages 10 to 60, with an exception at any age when both morphine and the heroin marker 6-monoacetylmorphine were found. The certificate selection had no age limit (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In England and Wales, the Office for National Statistics counts a death under a specific opioid only when a cause-of-death field in the coroner's Record of Inquest names it (Chen et al., 2025). Who decides differs as well: certifying physicians in Sweden and Norway, coroners in England and Wales, medical examiners or coroners in the US, and, for Norway's second register, local and central police (Fugelstad et al., 2020; Amundsen, 2017; Chen et al., 2025; Garnett et al., 2026). Matching the same deaths across two sources, the strongest evidence on this question, showed partial overlap in three countries. In Norway in 2007–2009, the Cause of Death Registry (822 deaths) and the police registry (562) together covered 929 people, of whom 455 (49%) were in both; 367 were only in the cause-of-death count, 74 police-registry deaths had a certified cause outside the European definition, and 33 had no match (39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or wrong identity numbers). The cause-of-death register covered Norwegian residents only; police covered unnatural deaths regardless of residence. Deaths only in the cause-of-death count were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had morphine or codeine, methadone, other synthetic opioids or stimulants rather than heroin as the first contributing-cause drug code, less often had an autopsy and more often occurred in hospitals or other institutions; autopsies were recorded for 715 of the 822, and the author states that neither source gives the correct figure, while judging the cause-of-death register more complete and broader and both sources probably too low (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden in 1994–2012, the certificate-based selection and the forensic toxicology register shared 4,238 of the 9,707 deaths in either, with 2,210 only in the toxicology register and 3,259 only in the certificate selection; a separate table, whose period is not stated, reports that 96% of toxicology-register deaths whose main drug was heroin were also in the certificate selection, against 23% where it was cannabis (THC). The authors conclude that comparing numbers or rates of drug deaths between countries misleads, while comparing trends is meaningful where investigation and certification have not changed, although they analysed no other country (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, where policy calls for full autopsy and toxicology of suspected drug or poison deaths, except in some tribal and federal jurisdictions unless invited (the actual share tested is not given), vital statistics and the medical investigator's records each held 1,046 of the 1,105 residents' poisoning deaths found in either, and 987 were in both. This was a broad poisoning category, including alcohol and carbon monoxide, not just drug poisoning. Of 59 deaths counted as poisonings only by vital statistics, 24 occurred in another state, 13 had never been reported to the medical investigator and 15 were natural deaths in the medical investigator's records (such as cirrhosis, sepsis or heart disease) that vital statistics coded as non-dependent drug use (the explanation involving use or abuse wording is the editors' inference from the paper's coding rule, not a reported reading of those individual certificates); of 59 counted only by the medical investigator, 37 had been coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning written only in Part II of the certificate, and 17 as other injuries (Landen et al., 2003). In a coroner-fed UK register's wider drug-related category for Liverpool (70 deaths, from deaths in 2004 and inquests in January to June 2005), 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity and 15 were of people living elsewhere; these groups can overlap, and residence is a separate feature, not shown to result from the wider drug-related definition (Beynon et al., 2007). Around 2000 in England and Wales, as cited by Webb et al. (2003), coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse numbered 605 (2000), the same register counted 1,296 drug-related deaths (2000) and the Office for National Statistics 2,943 deaths with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (1999). The linkage studies come from Norway, Sweden and one US state, the newest data are from 2012, and none comes from southern Europe. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: How is a death counted as a drug death? It depends on the country and the list. In the US count described here, drug poisoning must be the main cause on the death certificate. Drugs named in the cause-of-death or injury fields can each be counted, so one death can appear under several drugs. A Swedish list counted certain drugs found in tests, whatever the cause, mainly for people aged 10 to 60; its heroin-marker exception had no age limit. Doctors, coroners, medical examiners or police decide, depending on the place. The words they record affect the code. When researchers matched people across two lists, they did not fully agree: about half appeared on both in Norway, fewer than half in Sweden and about 9 in 10 in New Mexico. The New Mexico study counted other poisons too, such as alcohol and carbon monoxide. These are comparisons of three places, with different rules, and the newest linked data are from 2012.
magnitude: Definitions: US overdose deaths, ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85, Y10–Y14; drugs counted when mentioned in Part I, Part II or the injury description; 2023, 15 drug-specific counts sum to 179,965 for 106,352 deaths (1.69 times; 1.47 times in 2017; editors' arithmetic) (Garnett et al., 2026). Washington State 2003–2010: one code (T40.2) covered 2,725 poisoning deaths; six most common terms, not an exhaustive list, with overlapping mentions (Ossiander, 2014). Linkage: Norway 2007–2009, 929 people, 455 (49%) in both registers, 367 (40%) cause-of-death register only, 74 (8%) police register with a cause outside the European definition, 33 (4%) unmatched (Amundsen, 2017). Sweden 1994–2012: 4,238 of 9,707 in both the certificate selection and the toxicology register, 2,210 toxicology only, 3,259 certificate only; in a separate table with no stated period, capture of toxicology-register deaths by the certificate selection, heroin 96%, THC 23%; toxicology selection ages 10–60 except the heroin-marker cases at any age (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998, broad poisoning including alcohol and carbon monoxide: 1,046 in each source, 987 in both, 1,105 in either (94.7% and 89.3%); discordant deaths 59 each way (Landen et al., 2003). Liverpool 2004–2005: of 70 register deaths, 25 not from drug toxicity and 15 non-residents (overlapping categories) (Beynon et al., 2007). England and Wales, as cited: 605 coroners' verdicts (2000), 1,296 register deaths (2000), 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths (1999) (Webb et al., 2003). No intervals; counts of linked records.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded. The overlap counts come from matching complete registers on personal identity numbers (Norway, Sweden) or by hand with a case-by-case review of the discordant deaths (New Mexico) (cards sc_amundsen_2017, sc_fugelstad_2020, sc_landen_2003: JBI moderate, high and moderate). The reporting errors on those cards (a Swedish total printed as 6,648 and 6,448; one-death slips in New Mexico's union columns; a few cells of Norway's Table 1) change the overlaps by a few deaths, not their size, and the high rating of the Swedish card concerns its comparison with the Stockholm inventory, which this claim does not use. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them (NCHS, card sc_garnett_2026) or from the papers that describe their own registers. Complete-register linkage describes those records, not complete capture of all true drug-caused deaths; differing age, residence and cause definitions are not automatically errors.

inconsistency.note: The overlap ranges from about half (Norway: two different selecting bodies and definitions) to about nine in ten (New Mexico: two sources for the same poisoning deaths under similar definitions); the differences follow the definitions compared, as the claim says.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its place, source and years, and no overlap figure is carried to other countries or to today. The claim states that the linkage data end in 2012 and that none comes from southern Europe.

imprecision.note: Counts of linked records from complete registers; no sampling.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim about how deaths are counted and how far sources agree: starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: three independent linkage studies in different countries and systems (Norway, Sweden, New Mexico) agree that sources counting drug deaths in the same place and period disagree on substantial numbers of individual deaths, in both directions, and each traces the disagreement to definitions, certificate wording, residency rules and reporting routes; comparisons of two sources for the same deaths are the strongest evidence on this question. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them. The consensus statement (Goldberger et al., 2013) and the Liverpool register study (Beynon et al., 2007) illustrate definitions and add no rate; the England and Wales counts quoted by Webb et al. (2003) come from other sources and different years and are given only as cited. Status replicated: independent studies in three countries point the same way. Whether official counts miss drug deaths, and by how much, is a separate answer.

statement: Official records can miss a death altogether, or count it as a drug poisoning without identifying a particular drug. These are different gaps: the US statistical corrections described here address missing drug categories within deaths already counted as drug poisonings, not deaths missing from the overall overdose total. Comparisons in Sweden and New Mexico also found records that met one source's definition but not the other's, in both directions; the size and meaning of a gap depend on place, years and the reference used. In US coded death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had only unspecified-drug coding (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015; Ruhm, 2018). In overlapping national records, 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths had only unspecified-drug coding (22%; Buchanich et al., 2018), and 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths in 2010 had only that code (Slavova et al., 2015). These records do not establish which deaths had toxicology or whether an individual drug was absent from the original certificate text. By 2023, the share without a drug or drug-class code was 4.0%, down from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic); identifying a drug class still need not identify an individual drug. Ruhm's model used deaths with a specified drug category to estimate opioid involvement among deaths with only unspecified drugs, conditional on demographic and other covariates. The paper reports opioid counts 21% to 35% higher by year, including 33,091 to an estimated 39,999 in 2015; the maximum from its table is 35.7% by editors' arithmetic, so the printed range is approximate (Ruhm, 2018). A simpler reallocation within each state and year added about 70,000 potential unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015 (editors' table sum), with Pennsylvania's estimated 2015 rate changing from 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither correction checked the added drug assignments against toxicology or case files, and each can only add opioid assignments. A scoping review's national range largely cites Ruhm analyses of overlapping national files, with different periods and methods, not independent national replications (Gutkind et al., 2025). Certificate-text searches can separate names that a broad code merges but cannot supply a drug never written down (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). A review reports South Carolina's rate with prescription-type opioid codes rising from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014 as certificates listing specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% after a new name-collection process. The authors attribute this mainly to recording, citing personal correspondence, rather than separately measuring the contribution of changing drug exposure. The codes include synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl and do not show that a drug was prescribed (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). In Stockholm in 1985–1996, the certificate selection included 761 of 1,212 deaths in an individually assessed inventory. The inventory used a broad personal-history or illicit-drug definition, whatever the cause of death, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related; a missing inventory case is therefore not automatically a missed drug poisoning. The certificate selection also held 419 deaths absent from the inventory, of which 30 were found to be inventory omissions. The authors described some other certificate-only deaths involving drowning, alcohol or medicines; they did not describe every remaining case. Totals were close despite roughly a third of cases differing in each direction, and the inventory itself was incomplete (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, 37 deaths classified as poisonings by the medical investigator were coded as natural deaths in vital statistics, typically with poisoning only in Part II of the certificate. Conversely, 15 deaths treated as natural by the investigator had non-dependent drug-use coding in vital statistics. The explanation involving use or abuse wording is inferred from the paper's coding rule, not from presented text for all 15 certificates. This poisoning category includes alcohol and carbon monoxide as well as drugs; neither source was an independent reference standard (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted a specific opioid when named in a cause-of-death field of the Record of Inquest. The voluntary NPSUM programme received reports from over 90% of coroners, but not every death. Among its heroin/morphine deaths, ambiguous causes with that opioid implicated by the consulting toxicologist accounted for 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022 (endpoints, not the full range). Applying those shares to national counts without linking individual records gave 20,323 projected heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), against 13,471 counted. Official counts were 61% to 68% of the projections across the opioids studied; 96.8% of programme opioid deaths had multiple drugs detected. The intervals cover sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that its cases represent all deaths or the accuracy of causal attribution (Chen et al., 2025). Drug involvement is also different from a drug causing death. A death may appear under several drugs; in overlapping US records, at least 45% of unintentional opioid-coded deaths also had a non-opioid drug code, not necessarily a complete measure of multi-drug coding (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classified 802 of 1,037 accidental deaths reported by coroners to a drug-related register as direct overdose; that category was the default when recent drug use and no other explanation were recorded, so 77% is an upper limit under their information. Other classifications were acute physical events such as aspiration (74), toxicity with a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and acute infections (18). This was not a linked comparison with official overdose statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also exclude deaths: US overdose totals exclude chronic effects (Garnett et al., 2026), and Liverpool authors argue that definitions of the time excluded deaths from infections transmitted by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007, argument based on other studies). Non-opioid evidence is limited, not absent: a review reports larger gaps for cocaine and smaller ones for amphetamines in a Florida comparison of 2003–2017 (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand); the Swedish study also compares capture of deaths with amphetamine, cocaine or THC detected. Those are differences between sources, not validated rates of missed deaths caused by each drug. Most evidence here concerns historical US opioid records, not current counts everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss drug deaths? Some deaths are left out of a list. Others are counted as overdoses, but the records do not say which drug was involved. In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an unspecified-drug code. By 2023, about 4 in 100 had no drug or type-of-drug code. Models estimated more opioid involvement among deaths already counted as overdoses; they did not find deaths missing from the total, and their drug guesses were not checked against the case files. In Stockholm, two lists had similar totals but differed about which people belonged on them. One list also included deaths from other causes in people with a history of drug problems. In England and Wales, one estimate suggests the counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It used a sample of reports without matching each death across the lists, so that estimate may be wrong. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths. There is no single missing-death rate for every drug and place.
magnitude: US unspecified-drug coding: 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisonings 1999–2015, 26.0% in 2008 and 17.2% in 2015 (Ruhm, 2018); 97,159/438,607 unintentional overdoses, 22.2% (Buchanich et al., 2018; editors' arithmetic); 9,429/38,329 overdoses in 2010, 24.6% (Slavova et al., 2015; editors' arithmetic). No drug or drug-class code: 12.3% in 2017, 4.0% in 2023 (Garnett et al., 2026; editors' subtraction). Model estimates, not added deaths in the all-drug total: Ruhm printed range 21–35% more opioid-involved deaths (Table 1 maximum 35.7%, editors' calculation); 2015, 33,091 to 39,999, no computed intervals. Buchanich reallocation about 70,000 potential opioid deaths 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015 (editors' sum), Pennsylvania 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000. Stockholm 1985–1996: 761/1,212 inventory deaths in the certificate selection, 419 certificate-only, 30 confirmed inventory omissions; inventory included 151 hospital deaths (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998, broad poisoning: 37 investigator poisonings coded natural, 15 investigator natural deaths coded non-dependent drug use (Landen et al., 2003). England/Wales 2011–2022 unlinked projections: heroin/morphine 13,471 counted versus 20,323 projected (95% interval 19,382–21,358); projections not counted 32.5% fentanyl to 39.1% methadone (editors' calculations). Intervals cover sampling error only (Chen et al., 2025). Register composition: direct overdose 802/1,037 (77.3%, editors' calculation, an upper limit under the default rule), physical events 74, medical-condition groups 40+72=112 (editors' sum), injuries 31, infections 18 (Webb et al., 2003). Second-hand South Carolina rate 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 as named-drug certificates rose 57.7% to 94.4% (2013–2014; Slavova et al., 2019). Swedish presence-versus-certificate-selection capture, Table III period unstated: amphetamine 56%, cocaine 43%, THC 23%; not drug-specific causal miss rates (Fugelstad et al., 2020).

risk_of_bias.note: The drug-category corrections assume, without validation against toxicology/case files, that unspecified deaths resemble specified deaths conditional on the chosen covariates or state/year (Ruhm and Buchanich cards: high). Chen is an unlinked projection, and its sampling intervals exclude representativeness and attribution assumptions (high). The Stockholm inventory uses a broader personal-history definition, is itself incomplete and contains inconsistent accuracy/count reporting (high); New Mexico has no independent reference (moderate). Differences between definitions are not automatically causal classification errors.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: studies consistently find incomplete drug attribution or disagreement between sources, while the comparisons that allow both directions also find cases included by only one source. Sizes concern different quantities and definitions; they are not one common missing-death rate.

indirectness.note: Question concerns official counts generally; most evidence is historical US opioid coding, with Stockholm 1985–1996, New Mexico 1995–1998 and England/Wales unlinked projections 2011–2022. US coding completeness improved by 2023. Non-opioid comparisons exist in the Swedish paper and second-hand Florida report, but do not establish validated causal miss rates for stimulants, cannabis or new psychoactive substances everywhere.

imprecision.note: Counts are large. Ruhm did not compute intervals; Chen did, but its Wilson intervals cover sampling error rather than the central model/representation assumptions. No extra downgrade beyond the methodological limitations already assigned under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low, never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); minus one risk of bias and one indirectness, floored at very low. Same-death comparisons in Stockholm and New Mexico describe discordance under different definitions in both directions, without an independent causal reference standard. US unspecified-code figures describe already-counted overdoses; corrected drug assignments are model estimates, not extra deaths in the total. Overlapping NVSS analyses and their summaries in Gutkind/Slavova reviews are counted once, not as independent replication. The reviews also supply explicitly second-hand Florida/composition context. Replicated describes the direction of incomplete attribution/source disagreement across independent settings, not a shared magnitude or proven true-cause error rate. Chen contributes a combined heroin/morphine projection, with sampling intervals and an untested representativeness assumption. Certainty and status unchanged; draft until independent checks.

statement: Reviews of the same death-investigation files in Maryland and Victoria identified more heroin-related deaths under their own definitions than a search of certificate text or national heroin codes. Morphine recorded instead of heroin, general drug wording and coding or registration issues contributed, but the comparisons do not validate a universal rate of deaths caused by heroin. An England and Wales projection addresses a different quantity: combined heroin/morphine deaths, not heroin misnamed as morphine. In Maryland in 2012–2015, the authors' search of the state's medical-examiner certificates found heroin named in 1,130 overdose deaths. A protocol developed by state agencies identified 2,182 using certificate text, toxicology and scene evidence: heroin on the certificate, a heroin-specific metabolite in tests, morphine with quinine, or morphine/unspecified certification together with scene evidence suggesting heroin. It excluded cases whose scene notes suggested prescription morphine. Because it retained every certificate naming heroin, it could only add heroin assignments. The 1,052 additions had morphine certified in 804 cases, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% of protocol-defined deaths (95% interval 49.7–53.9), from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often among people aged 55 or older (41.9%), women (35.1%) and non-Hispanic Black women (25.9%). The authors acknowledge that some added cases, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin-related (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, the authors applied their earlier heroin-attribution model to closed coronial files, using toxicology plus circumstances, clinical and pathological evidence in the context of cause of death. It selected 243 deaths, with the heroin-specific marker in 180; the remaining 63 relied on morphine findings and investigative evidence (editors' subtraction). Of those selected, 235 were toxicity deaths and eight were misadventure deaths after heroin intoxication. Those eight are outside the national poisoning/dependence underlying-cause definition described in this comparison, so not every difference is a recording error. National data held 165 deaths with the heroin code, 161 inside the model-defined group and four judged coincidental by the model; 82 of the 243 lacked the heroin code, a net difference of 78 between totals. The Victorian attribution groups counted heroin named either in the cause of death or in the NCIS object-causing-death field. Of 191 toxicity deaths attributed to heroin on that basis, 37 lacked its code. The authors describe generic certification with drugs named only in the object field, morphine written as the cause with heroin only as the object, and complications listed first. They do not print a cross-tabulation separating wording issues from late registration in these groups. Of 39 deaths attributed to morphine or another opioid, 34 lacked the heroin code; all five generic-toxicity deaths lacked it. Twenty model-selected deaths had no code at all, which the authors judged most reasonably due to late initial registration and no coding assessment, not simply certificate wording. Since the study years, associated-cause toxicity codes have also become subject to revision when new information arrives, limiting application to newer statistics (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted 13,471 deaths naming heroin or morphine in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest. NPSUM's coroner reports and toxicology reports identified a further share with an ambiguous drug cause in which a consulting toxicologist implicated heroin/morphine: 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022, the endpoint years rather than a range across all years. Applying those shares nationally, without linking individual records, projected 20,323 combined heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), about 51% above the ONS count (editors' calculation). These intervals address sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that those shares represent all cases. The median number of drugs detected in programme heroin/morphine deaths rose from four to six; detection is not proof that every drug caused death (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports further comparisons second-hand. In Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin-involved deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review, while morphine-involved deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine-involved deaths from 34 to five; the decreases exceed the heroin increase, so these cannot be read as a one-for-one transfer between exclusive groups. In New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin. In SUDORS data for 38 states and Washington DC in 2018–2019, 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths had only morphine on the certificate; enhanced definitions raised the heroin share from 80.2% to 93.3%. These primary studies were not read here, and their enhanced categories are not an independent test of true causal attribution (Gutkind et al., 2025). Heroin is rapidly converted to 6-acetylmorphine and then morphine; the specific marker may be absent after delayed death or change in stored specimens, so morphine after death can have several origins (Stam et al., 2019, describing earlier literature). National statistics also warn that a morphine mention may reflect heroin rather than direct morphine use (Garnett et al., 2026). A US medical-examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin without an attached citation; for a morphine-to-codeine ratio above one as possible evidence of heroin use it cites three empirical studies, but does not report the rule's diagnostic accuracy. Those studies were not independently read here (Davis et al., 2020). The Maryland and Victorian reference definitions were not validated against an independent causal standard, and the English and Welsh estimate is unlinked and combines two drugs. These historical findings cannot specify a current heroin-caused-death miss rate everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss heroin deaths? In Maryland and Victoria, closer file reviews linked more deaths to heroin than certificate text or national codes did. Heroin turns into morphine in the body, and some records said morphine or mixed drugs instead. In Maryland, certificates named heroin in about 52 out of 100 deaths the fuller protocol linked to heroin. In Victoria, about 34 out of 100 model-selected deaths lacked the heroin code; a few coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance. The model also included some deaths outside the national poisoning definition. The reviews used their own rules, with no independent check of whether heroin caused each death. In England and Wales, a separate estimate suggests about half as many again as counted, but it combines heroin and morphine and does not match each death across the lists. These are different comparisons, not one missing-death rate.
magnitude: Maryland 2012–2015 (Horon et al., 2018; authors' certificate-text search versus enhanced protocol): 1,130 deaths with heroin on the certificate against 2,182 by the enhanced protocol (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths, a total not defined in the paper); added 1,052: morphine certified 804, no specific drug 193, other substance 55; certificates named heroin in 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths, 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of non-Hispanic Black women. Victoria 2012–2013 (Stam et al., 2019): 243 model-defined deaths (235 toxicity, 8 misadventure outside the selected national underlying-cause definition; 6-acetylmorphine in 180) against 165 with the heroin code; code missing from 82 (34%, editors' arithmetic); 4 coded deaths judged coincidental; heroin attributed in cause-of-death or NCIS object field, coded 154 of 191; morphine or other opioid certified 5 of 39 coded; generic 0 of 5; 20 with no code, authors' likely late-initial-registration explanation. England and Wales 2011–2022 (Chen et al., 2025; unlinked projection): combined heroin/morphine ONS 13,471 against 20,323 projected (95% interval 19,382–21,358) (about 51% more, editors' calculation); 2011 574 against 813 (95% CI 767–868); 2022 1,264 against 1,980 (95% interval 1,894–2,074). Second-hand (Gutkind et al., 2025): Allegheny County heroin 171 to 245, morphine 132 to 41, codeine 34 to 5; New York City 84 of 118 opiate-intoxication deaths attributed to heroin. SUDORS 38 states and DC, 2018–2019, second-hand in Gutkind: morphine-only certificate wording in 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths; enhanced heroin share 80.2% to 93.3%. Reference standards unvalidated; no intervals for Victorian counts. Chen reports Wilson intervals for projections, covering sampling error only; Table 1 values used where the text differs.

risk_of_bias.note: Maryland and Victorian reference definitions are not independently validated causal standards. They combine toxicological markers and investigative evidence; Stam evaluates them in the context of cause of death, so it is too absolute to say no causal judgment occurred. Who reviewed and blinding to codes are not described in the inherited Horon extraction or supplied Stam methods (cards moderate). Victoria also uses a broader misadventure definition and has late-registration/coding limits. England/Wales is an unlinked combined heroin/morphine projection (high); its sampling intervals exclude representation/attribution assumptions. A stricter causal or harmonised definition could change the gaps.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: same-file heroin comparisons in Maryland and Victoria and second-hand US comparisons point toward incomplete heroin attribution. They do not share a common magnitude or all measure one mechanism: England/Wales measures combined heroin/morphine ambiguous wording, not substitution of morphine for heroin.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each setting, period and reference is identified; historical file-review findings, second-hand review summaries and combined heroin/morphine projections are distinguished. Presence, use and causal attribution are not treated as equivalent, and definition/registration changes limit application to current statistics.

imprecision.note: Counts of hundreds to thousands of deaths; the Maryland shares have narrow intervals.

Maryland and Victoria compare the same files under different rules, the most direct comparisons here, but their reference definitions are unvalidated.
